claim: Pyomyositis is a severe bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, commonly affecting children in tropical regions.
source: Pyomyositis is a severe bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, commonly affecting children in tropical regions, predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about pyomyositis.

claim: Pyomyositis is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
source: Pyomyositis is a severe bacterial infection of skeletal muscle, commonly affecting children in tropical regions, predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: The study conducted a genome-wide association study of S. aureus cultured from 101 children with pyomyositis and 417 children with asymptomatic nasal carriage.
source: To understand the contribution of bacterial genomic factors to pyomyositis, we conducted a genome-wide association study of S. aureus cultured from 101 children with pyomyositis and 417 children with asymptomatic nasal carriage attending the Angkor Hospital for Children, Cambodia.
evidence: This describes the study design and sample sizes used in the research.

claim: The estimated heritability of pyomyositis in the bacterial population is 63.8% (95% CI 49.2–78.4%).
source: We found a strong relationship between bacterial genetic variation and pyomyositis, with estimated heritability 63.8% (95% CI 49.2–78.4%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the GWAS analysis.

claim: The presence of the Panton–Valentine leucocidin (PVL) locus increased the odds of pyomyositis 130-fold (p=10-17.9).
source: The presence of the Panton–Valentine leucocidin (PVL) locus increased the odds of pyomyositis 130-fold (p=10-17.9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the GWAS showing the association strength.

claim: The PVL-coding sequence and the sequence immediately upstream together explained over 99.9% of heritability (95% CI 93.5–100%).
source: Together these regions explained over 99.9% of heritability (95% CI 93.5–100%).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the heritability analysis.

claim: Staphylococcal pyomyositis is critically dependent on a single toxin, like tetanus and diphtheria.
source: Our results establish staphylococcal pyomyositis, like tetanus and diphtheria, as critically dependent on a single toxin and demonstrate the potential for association studies to identify specific bacterial genes promoting severe human disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results, comparing pyomyositis to other toxin-mediated diseases.

claim: In up to 90% of pyomyositis cases, it is caused by S. aureus.
source: In up to 90% of cases, it is caused by a single bacterial pathogen, Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) (Chauhan et al., 2004; Verma, 2016; Bickels et al., 2002; Moriarty et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Unlike infections of the skin and superficial soft tissues, the skin and subcutaneous tissues are not usually involved in pyomyositis.
source: Unlike infections of the skin and superficial soft tissues, the skin and subcutaneous tissues are not usually involved in pyomyositis, by contrast to intense inflammation in the infected muscles (Chauhan et al., 2004; Verma, 2016).
evidence: This is a clinical characteristic of pyomyositis supported by citations.

claim: Pyomyositis is thought to arise from haematogenous seeding of bacteria from blood to muscle.
source: Pyomyositis is thought to arise from haematogenous seeding of bacteria from blood to muscle (Verma, 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis about the pathogenesis supported by a citation.

claim: The incidence of pyomyositis in the USA doubled during an epidemic of community-associated methicillin resistant S. aureus (CA-MRSA).
source: There is evidence that some S. aureus strains have heightened propensity to cause pyomyositis – the incidence in the USA doubled during an epidemic of community-associated methicillin resistant S. aureus (CA-MRSA) (Pannaraj et al., 2006)
evidence: This is an epidemiological observation supported by a citation.

claim: PVL is a bipartite pore-forming toxin comprising the co-expressed LukF-PV and LukS-PV proteins.
source: PVL is a bipartite pore-forming toxin comprising the co-expressed LukF-PV and LukS-PV proteins (Löffler et al., 2010; Boakes et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PVL structure supported by citations.

claim: The coding sequence for PVL, lukSF-PV, is usually carried on bacteriophages.
source: The coding sequence for PVL, lukSF-PV, is usually carried on bacteriophages, (Shallcross et al., 2013; Löffler et al., 2010), which facilitate lukSF-PV exchange between lineages (McCarthy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PVL genetics supported by citations.

claim: Bacteriophages facilitate lukSF-PV exchange between lineages.
source: The coding sequence for PVL, lukSF-PV, is usually carried on bacteriophages, (Shallcross et al., 2013; Löffler et al., 2010), which facilitate lukSF-PV exchange between lineages (McCarthy et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation describing horizontal gene transfer.

claim: The mechanism of PVL toxicity involves cell lysis in human myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils, by insertion into the cellular membrane.
source: The mechanism of PVL toxicity has been shown to involve cell lysis in human myeloid cells, particularly neutrophils, by insertion into the cellular membrane, (Niemann et al., 2018) leading the tissue to release inflammatory neutrophil products (Spaan et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PVL mechanism supported by citations.

claim: Neutrophil lysis is mediated by PVL binding to target complement receptors C5aR.
source: Neutrophil lysis is mediated by PVL binding to target complement receptors C5aR; in binding, PVL has both toxic and immunomodulatory effects, as it also inhibits C5a mediated immune activation (Sina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PVL mechanism supported by a citation.

claim: PVL has both toxic and immunomodulatory effects by inhibiting C5a mediated immune activation.
source: Neutrophil lysis is mediated by PVL binding to target complement receptors C5aR; in binding, PVL has both toxic and immunomodulatory effects, as it also inhibits C5a mediated immune activation (Sina et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about PVL function supported by a citation.

claim: Small case series have reported a high prevalence of PVL among pyomyositis-causing S. aureus.
source: Although small case series testing for candidate genes have reported a high prevalence of PVL among pyomyositis-causing S. aureus, (Pannaraj et al., 2006; Sina et al., 2013; García et al., 2013)
evidence: This is a summary of previous research supported by citations.

claim: A detailed meta-analysis found no evidence for an increased rate of musculoskeletal infection (or other invasive disease) in PVL-positive bacteria versus controls.
source: a detailed meta-analysis found no evidence for an increased rate of musculoskeletal infection (or other invasive disease) in PVL-positive bacteria versus controls (Shallcross et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a result from a previous meta-analysis supported by a citation.

claim: 86/101 (85%) of pyomyositis cases were caused by CC-121 bacteria.
source: Notably, 86/101 (85%) of pyomyositis cases were caused by CC-121 bacteria, whereas no pyomyositis cases were caused by the next two most commonly carried lineages, sequence type (ST)−834 and CC-45 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No pyomyositis cases were caused by ST-834 and CC-45 lineages.
source: Notably, 86/101 (85%) of pyomyositis cases were caused by CC-121 bacteria, whereas no pyomyositis cases were caused by the next two most commonly carried lineages, sequence type (ST)−834 and CC-45 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PC 1 distinguished CC-121 from ST-834 and showed the strongest association with case/control status (p=10-29.6).
source: PC 1, which distinguished CC-121 (the most common pyomyositis lineage) from ST-834 (which was only found in carriage), showed the strongest association with case/control status (p=10-29.6, Wald test).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the principal component analysis.

claim: PC 20 differentiated a sub-lineage of CC-121 within which no cases were seen (p=10-13.9).
source: The strongest association was with PC 20, which differentiated a sub-lineage of CC-121 within which no cases were seen (p=10-13.9)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the principal component analysis.

claim: PC 2 distinguished CC-45 from the rest of the species (p=10-4.9).
source: and PC 2, which distinguished CC-45 from the rest of the species (p=10-4.9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the principal component analysis.

claim: 10.7 million unique kmers were found variably present across the bacterial genomes.
source: We found 10.7 million unique kmers variably present across the bacterial genomes.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the kmer analysis.

claim: 9175 kmers were significantly associated with case/control status after correction for multiple testing (10-6.8 ≤ p ≤ 10-21.4).
source: In total, 9175 kmers were significantly associated with case/control status after correction for multiple testing (10-6.8 ≤ p ≤ 10-21.4; Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the GWAS shown in Figure 2A.

claim: 9,074/9,175 (98.9%) of significant kmers localised to a 45.7 kb region spanning an integrated prophage with 95% nucleotide identity to φSLT.
source: When mapped to the de novo assembly of a CC121 isolate from pyomyositis (PYO2134), the vast majority of these kmers (9,074/9,175; 98.9%) localised to a 45.7 kb region spanning an integrated prophage with 95% nucleotide identity to φSLT (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is a result from mapping kmers to the reference genome shown in Figure 2B.

claim: 9,173/9,175 (99.98%) significant kmers were found at an increased frequency in pyomyositis.
source: Most (9,173/9,175; 99.98%) significant kmers were found at an increased frequently in pyomyositis, with odds ratios (OR) ranging from 2.7 to 139.8, indicating that the presence of each was associated with increased risk of disease.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the association analysis.

claim: The odds ratios for significant kmers ranged from 2.7 to 139.8.
source: Most (9,173/9,175; 99.98%) significant kmers were found at an increased frequently in pyomyositis, with odds ratios (OR) ranging from 2.7 to 139.8, indicating that the presence of each was associated with increased risk of disease.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the association analysis.

claim: The presence of bacteriophage φSLT was strongly associated with pyomyositis.
source: The presence of bacteriophage φSLT was thus strongly associated with pyomyositis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the kmer mapping results.

claim: 1630 kmers tagging the presence of the lukSF-PV coding sequences were present in 98/101 (97%) pyomyositis cases and 84/417 (20%) carriage controls.
source: 1630 kmers tagging the presence of the lukSF-PV coding sequences (CDS) were highly significantly associated with disease, being present in 98/101 (97%) pyomyositis cases and 84/417 (20%) carriage controls (unadjusted OR 129.5, p=10-17.9).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the kmer analysis.

claim: The unadjusted odds ratio for lukSF-PV coding sequence kmers was 129.5 (p=10-17.9).
source: 1630 kmers tagging the presence of the lukSF-PV coding sequences (CDS) were highly significantly associated with disease, being present in 98/101 (97%) pyomyositis cases and 84/417 (20%) carriage controls (unadjusted OR 129.5, p=10-17.9).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the association analysis.

claim: Kmers tagging variation in the 389 bp region immediately upstream of the PVL CDS were strongly associated with disease (p=10-21.4).
source: Kmers tagging variation in the 389 bp region immediately upstream of the CDS were also strongly associated with disease (p=10-21.4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the association analysis.

claim: The most significant upstream kmers were co-present with the CDS in 98/101 (97.0%) cases but present in only 79/417 (18.9%) controls, producing an OR of 140.
source: The most significant of these kmers were co-present with the CDS in the same cases (98/101, 97.0%), but present in fewer controls (79/417, 18.9%), producing an OR of 140.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the association analysis.

claim: Long-read Oxford Nanopore sequencing was performed on 37 genomes with incomplete or discontinuous assembly upstream of the PVL locus.
source: To improve the accuracy of this region of the assembled genomes we performed long-read Oxford Nanopore sequencing on the 37 genomes with incomplete or discontinuous assembly upstream of the PVL CDS.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach taken in the study.

claim: When improved assemblies were introduced, the signal of association upstream of the PVL CDS was no more significant than within the CDS.
source: When these improved assemblies were introduced, the signal of association upstream of the PVL CDS was no more significant than within the CDS (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis using hybrid assemblies shown in Figure 2C.

claim: All isolates with kmers mapping to the PVL CDS had 98% or more coverage for the PVL CDS genes in de novo assembly.
source: All isolates with kmers mapping to the PVL CDS had 98% or more coverage for the PVL CDS genes in de novo assembly (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a result from the assembly analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: When the most significant kmer pattern was included as a covariate, the remaining heritability not explained by other factors was estimated at 0.0% (95% CI 0–2.5%).
source: When the presence or absence of the most significant kmer pattern, a set of kmers with an identical pattern of presence in the population, all of which mapped to the PVL region, was included as a covariate in GEMMA, the remaining heritability not explained by other factors was estimated and found to be 0.0% (95% CI 0–2.5%).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the heritability analysis.

claim: The point estimate for heritability not explained by PVL-tagging kmers is reduced by 100% (95% CI 93.5–100%).
source: Thus, the point estimate for heritability (not explained by the inclusion of PVL-tagging kmers) is reduced by 100% (95% CI 93.5–100%), meaning we have little evidence for any remaining heritability in case/control status.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the heritability analysis.

claim: The PVL region was absent from only three pyomyositis cases (in lineages CC-88, CC-1 and CC-121).
source: Its absence from only three cases (in lineages CC-88, CC-1 and CC-121) suggested that the PVL region approached necessity for development of pyomyositis in the current setting in Cambodian children
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the study data.

claim: The PVL region approached necessity for development of pyomyositis in Cambodian children.
source: Its absence from only three cases (in lineages CC-88, CC-1 and CC-121) suggested that the PVL region approached necessity for development of pyomyositis in the current setting in Cambodian children
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that only 3 cases lacked PVL.

claim: The presence of PVL in 20% of controls indicated that PVL-associated pyomyositis is incompletely penetrant.
source: while its presence in 20% of controls indicated that PVL-associated pyomyositis is incompletely penetrant, that is presence of the PVL region does not always lead to disease.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observation that PVL is present in asymptomatic carriers.

claim: PVL genes were carried on multiple genetic backgrounds in this population.
source: PVL genes were carried on multiple genetic backgrounds in this population, and the phage backgrounds vary by clonal complex.
evidence: This is a result from the phage analysis.

claim: The phage backgrounds vary by clonal complex.
source: PVL genes were carried on multiple genetic backgrounds in this population, and the phage backgrounds vary by clonal complex.
evidence: This is a result from the phage analysis.

claim: Sequences with >95% homology to four of seven phages were found in the population.
source: We find sequences with >95% homology to four of these seven phages in the population.
evidence: This is a result from the BLAST analysis of phage sequences.

claim: A single coding region together with the upstream sequence are all but necessary for the development of pyomyositis.
source: In this study, we found a strong association between pyomyositis, a highly distinctive tropical infection of skeletal muscle in children, and Panton-Valentine leukocidin, a bacterial toxin commonly carried by bacteriophages. We found that a single coding region together with the upstream sequence are all but necessary for the development of pyomyositis
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: The sporadic presence of PVL is associated with pyomyositis in otherwise low-frequency strains.
source: its sporadic presence is associated with pyomyositis in otherwise low-frequency strains, and its absence is associated with asymptomatic carriage in a high-propensity strain.
evidence: This is a result from the study data.

claim: The absence of PVL is associated with asymptomatic carriage in a high-propensity strain.
source: its sporadic presence is associated with pyomyositis in otherwise low-frequency strains, and its absence is associated with asymptomatic carriage in a high-propensity strain.
evidence: This is a result from the study data.

claim: PVL appears to be carried on multiple phage backgrounds in this population.
source: PVL appears to be carried on multiple phage backgrounds in this population, but PVL-positive lineages generally carry a single phage type, as expected given the observed strain restriction of phages in S. aureus (Xia and Wolz, 2014; Stegger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result from the phage analysis.

claim: PVL-positive lineages generally carry a single phage type.
source: PVL appears to be carried on multiple phage backgrounds in this population, but PVL-positive lineages generally carry a single phage type, as expected given the observed strain restriction of phages in S. aureus (Xia and Wolz, 2014; Stegger et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a result from the phage analysis supported by citations.

claim: The locally common PVL-positive CC-121 lineage contributes most strongly to the prevalence of pyomyositis in Cambodian children.
source: The locally common PVL-positive CC-121 lineage contributes most strongly to the prevalence of pyomyositis in Cambodian children.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study results.

claim: All the pyomyositis cases were MSSA (methicillin-sensitive S. aureus).
source: Despite the emergence of CA-MRSA in carriage in Cambodia (Nickerson et al., 2011), all the pyomyositis cases were MSSA (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the study data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Skeletal muscle abscesses are rarely observed in experimental models of bacteraemia, unless there is preceding muscle trauma.
source: The establishment of muscle abscesses is a critical step in the pathogenesis of pyomyositis, but unlike renal, hepatic and splenic abscesses, skeletal muscle abscesses are rarely observed in experimental models of bacteraemia, unless there is preceding muscle trauma (Miyake, 1904).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: S. aureus strains containing PVL show increased duration of bacteraemia in a rabbit model of sepsis.
source: S. aureus strains containing PVL show increased duration of bacteraemia in a rabbit model of sepsis, (Xia and Wolz, 2014) and result in larger muscle abscesses (Tseng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from animal models supported by a citation.

claim: S. aureus strains containing PVL result in larger muscle abscesses in animal models.
source: S. aureus strains containing PVL show increased duration of bacteraemia in a rabbit model of sepsis, (Xia and Wolz, 2014) and result in larger muscle abscesses (Tseng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is experimental evidence from animal models supported by a citation.

claim: PVL has been found strongly bound to necrotic muscle in an individual with myositis associated with necrotizing fasciitis.
source: PVL has been found strongly bound to necrotic muscle in an individual with myositis associated with necrotizing fasciitis (Lehman et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a clinical observation supported by a citation.

claim: Vaccines that generate neutralising anti-toxin antibodies against PVL might protect human populations specifically against pyomyositis.
source: Therefore, vaccines that generate neutralising anti-toxin antibodies against PVL (Landrum et al., 2017) might protect human populations specifically against this common tropical disease.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the study results and supported by a citation.

claim: Antibiotics which decrease toxin expression may offer specific clinical benefit in treating pyomyositis.
source: These results also raise the hypothesis that antibiotics which decrease toxin expression, and have been recommended in some PVL-associated infections, (Saeed et al., 2018) may offer specific clinical benefit in treating pyomyositis.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the study results and supported by a citation.

claim: 106 clinical episodes of pyomyositis were identified, in 101 individuals.
source: 106 clinical episodes of pyomyositis were identified, in 101 individuals, and we included the earliest episode from each individual.
evidence: This describes the sample collection for the study.

claim: Controls were selected from carriers in two cohorts: 222 of 519 from the 2008 cohort and 195 of 261 from the 2012 cohort.
source: We selected controls from carriers in these two cohorts using the excel randomization function: 222 of 519 from the 2008 cohort and 195 of 261 from the 2012 cohort.
evidence: This describes the control selection for the study.

claim: The median kmer length used in assembly was 123 bp (IQR 119–123).
source: The median kmer length was 123 bp (IQR 119–123).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the assembly process.

claim: Strains that shared 6 of 7 MLST loci were considered to be in the same Clonal Complex.
source: Strains that shared 6 of 7 MLST loci were considered to be in the same Clonal Complex (Feil et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a methodological definition supported by a citation.

claim: A median of 2,801,000 kmers per isolate were identified (IQR 2,778,000–2,837,000).
source: We identified a median of 2,801,000 kmers per isolate, including variably present kmers and kmers common to all genomes (IQR 2,778,000–2,837,000).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the kmer counting analysis.

claim: The study found 101 kmers significantly associated with pyomyositis that mapped to regions outside the PVL-carrying prophage.
source: Out of 9175 kmers significantly associated with pyomyositis, we only found 101 kmers related to regions outside the PVL-carrying prophage (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a result from the GWAS analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Two kmers mapping near 0.2 Mb showed homology to platelet adhesin sraP by BLAST.
source: Two kmers mapping at a position near 0.2 Mb in the PYO2014 reference genome showed homology to platelet adhesin sraP by BLAST.
evidence: This is a result from the BLAST analysis of significant kmers.

claim: Thirty-five kmers mapping to a 50 bp non-coding fragment at 0.6 Mb showed homology to an MSSA476 intergenic sequence between adhesin-encoding sdrC and sdrD by BLAST.
source: Thirty-five kmers mapping to a 50 bp non-coding fragment at 0.6 Mb and two kmers mapping to 2.8 Mb showed homology to an MSSA476 intergenic sequence between adhesin-encoding sdrC and sdrD by BLAST.
evidence: This is a result from the BLAST analysis of significant kmers.

claim: Sixty-one kmers mapping to a 61 bp non-coding region at 2.7 Mb showed homology to an MSSA476 intergenic sequence between acetyltransferase-encoding genes SAS2453 and SAS2454 by BLAST.
source: Sixty-one kmers mapping to a 61 bp non-coding region at 2.7 Mb showed homology to an MSSA476 intergenic sequence between acetyltransferase-encoding genes SAS2453 and SAS2454 by BLAST.
evidence: This is a result from the BLAST analysis of significant kmers.

claim: The other signals outside the PVL region were short, fragmentary and mostly non-coding.
source: In conclusion, these other signals were short, fragmentary and mostly non-coding so we did not investigate them further.
evidence: This is a characterization of the non-PVL associated signals.

claim: Bacterial GWAS can pinpoint virulence variants when MGEs act to unravel linkage disequilibrium, if effect sizes are sufficiently strong.
source: Bacterial GWAS can pinpoint virulence variants when MGEs act to unravel linkage disequilibrium, if effect sizes are sufficiently strong.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the utility of bacterial GWAS drawn from the study results.

claim: PVL may facilitate bacterial seeding to muscles via the bloodstream and tropism for muscular infection.
source: These observations support the hypothesis that PVL may facilitate bacterial seeding to muscles via the bloodstream and tropism for muscular infection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the study results and previous literature.

claim: The study demonstrates the potential for association studies to identify specific bacterial genes promoting severe human disease.
source: More generally, our study provides an example of how microbial GWAS can be used to elucidate the pathogenesis of bacterial infections and identify specific virulence genes associated with human disease.
evidence: This is a general conclusion about the utility of GWAS drawn from the study.
